newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street nervous about payroll data due Friday.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street nervous about payroll data due Friday.

text.p: Wall Street jitters over March payroll data due Friday morning was one factor in Wednesday's continued slump in stock prices, analysts said.

While some players had been hoping stocks would stabilize ahead of the number, the growing nervousness contributed to a volatile session. "All of the other numbers have been strong, how is it possible the payroll numbers will show weakness?" said one trader. A string of data showing a resilient U.S. economy has fanned fears that last week's hike in short term interest rates will only be the first in a series of increases.
A.C. Moore, chief investment strategist with Principal Financial Securities, Dallas, said while the payroll number may show a slowing, the wage component of the data could be "relatively strong."
Wage inflation was a key concern of Wall Street even before Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan moved to raise the Federal Funds rate March 25.

The 30-year U.S. Treasury bond edged up only 1/32 Wednesday to yield 7.07 percent. Asked why bonds seemed to be calmer than stocks, Moore said it reflected the many nuances in stocks while bonds focus mainly on interest rates.

"The bond market has stabilized but the stock market has many more elements in it," said Moore. He pointed to momentum players, who buy stocks mainly because they are moving up and accelerate the rise. When their stocks stop moving up, the momentum players tend to head for the exit in unison.

Another trader pointed to the popularity of index funds, which try to duplicate the performance of the Standard & Poor's 500 stock index. This trader said that these funds tend to be almost fully invested, so if a drop in the market triggers redemptions, the funds have to sell stocks which only adds fuel to the decline.

Moore said another factor is that stocks are correcting downward fron a point of overvaluation. He said while a five to 10 percent downward adjustment may have been the normal move, the overvaluation has set the market up for a move that could be as much as 12 percent. The Dow industrials have already fallen eight percent from a closing high of 7085 on March 11. The Dow fell 94 points to 6517 on Wednesday.

Moore said that looking further out, the economic backdrop of benign inflation combined with growth still has not changed. And he said the investment of retirement funds by Americans remains a positive factor for the markets.
